idiom_name: lazy iterator adapters - std::iter::successors/from_fn as the unfold, Iterator::fold/try_fold as the fold
implementation_notes: Rust's iterator protocol is the pattern built into the language: std::iter::successors(seed, next) and std::iter::from_fn construct the unfold lazily, Iterator::fold, try_fold and reduce consume it, and adaptors such as scan, map and take_while compose both sides without ever collecting. Adaptors are lazy, so each item is produced and consumed in the same step, and the chain is monomorphized into a single loop - the fused recursion with no intermediate Vec and no dynamic dispatch (the zero-cost abstraction claim). Collecting into a Vec is the explicit opt-in to materialization, and try_fold/collect over Result is the idiomatic way to give the fused recursion an early exit.
code_sketch:
fn factorial(n: u64) -> Option<u64> {              // fused: unfold then fold
    std::iter::successors(Some(n), |&s| (s > 1).then(|| s - 1))
        .try_fold(1u64, u64::checked_mul)          // no Vec is allocated
}
pitfalls: Iterator adaptors are single-use and Rust enforces it at the type level, but calling a helper twice silently re-runs the whole unfold - bind the chain once when the computation is expensive.
Deeply nested or infinite adaptor chains are heap-free but not stack-free: a recursive closure that captures itself (or successors over a recursive structure) can still overflow.
try_fold/collect over Option/Result stop at the first None/Err, which is the idiomatic early exit - but the adapter is consumed, so subsequent use needs a fresh iterator.
Long chains bloat monomorphized code and compile times; Box<dyn Iterator> trades that away for dynamic dispatch, so measure before accepting the trade.
